name: Olga Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying economics and business at Eastgate University and living at home in Pell Green with my mum and my grandad. A normal week is lectures on four days, a call-centre shift on Wednesday evening and Saturday, and tutoring two school kids in maths on Sunday afternoon. I plan all of it in a shared calendar that my AI assistant helps me fill.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the part of university you like most so far?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mum works as a care assistant and Grandad has a small pension, so there's no spare money for me. I got top results, and I've got loans for the fees and a bit of a bursary. I use AI every day for summaries, practice questions and even to rehearse interviews. I like trying new tools, and I sometimes get annoyed when classmates avoid them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. That one's called AI Plateau. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine and it doesn't surprise me. A lot of the hype is from people selling tools. I'd say learn them anyway, because even small time savings add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel okay about my own situation, but not relaxed. The call centre already uses a chatbot for simple questions, so fewer of us are needed in the evenings. If my shifts shrink, I'd lose a chunk of my spending money, and I've got about a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my current routine and use the tools to speed up the dull parts of study. I'd try to get more tutoring pupils, because that pays better than the call centre. And I'd put a bit of my wage into a savings pot each month, so I have two months' cover by Christmas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit busy. I like having a plan, and I like being useful. I'd say mildly positive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're comfortable with the tools. Would a flat future feel boring or comforting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, comforting. A flat future means I can plan a degree and a job the way I thought I would. But I'd still be annoyed by the debt number, flat or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your money if the call centre loses its evening shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for more tutoring hours, and start looking at paid research assistant jobs. I'd also ask my aunt about weekend work at her accountants' office. I wouldn't ask Mum for money, since she needs it for the bills.

say: I'd say it doesn't surprise me, and a lot of the hype comes from people **selling tools**.
I'd tell friends to learn the tools anyway.
think: The call centre already uses a chatbot for simple questions, so **evening shifts** could shrink.
I've got only about **a month** saved.
do: Use the tools to speed up the dull parts of **study**.
Take on more **tutoring** pupils, which pays better than the call centre.
Build **two months'** cover in a savings pot by Christmas.
feel: Fine and a bit busy, **mildly positive**, because I like having a plan.
S0.quote: A flat future means I can plan a degree and a job the way I thought I would.
fieldNote: Her unease is about **shifts** and a **thin cushion**, but she has a clear route to extra income.
She expects the call centre to shrink even in a quiet scenario.
Positive about tools but not naive about the money.

steps.text: Take on three more maths tutoring pupils
Save a hundred pounds a month for a two-month cushion
Use an AI tool to make practice questions for my study

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. That one's called Steady Disruption. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, so use it. I'd tell classmates to learn the basics and I'd show them how. I'd also say employers should help with training, not just expect people to figure it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Economics and business are exactly the thinking work the card talks about. Fewer entry-level analyst roles will exist in three years, I expect. But I'm also well placed. I'd already be good with the tools, and I can explain numbers to people, which isn't easy to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build projects that show what I can do: a data analysis of local shop prices, a tutoring website, and a small research blog. I'd apply for placements in my second year and seek firms that value people who know both the tools and the business. I'd keep the tutoring, but I'd leave the call centre if it shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit buzzy. Part of me finds it exciting, and part of me is aware that exciting isn't the same as safe. I'd call it focused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which jobs on that card do you see changing around you already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The call centre is the clearest example. They've cut their chat team, and customer emails are now first answered by a bot. Also the admin jobs advertised for graduates have gone down. I've noticed because I look at job boards for fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to classmates who refuse to touch the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say you don't have to love them, but you can't ignore them. A tool is like a calculator. You still have to know when the answer looks wrong. I'd rather be good at that than be afraid.

say: I'd say it's here, so **use it**, and I'd show classmates the basics.
Employers should help with **training**, not just expect people to figure it out.
think: Economics is the thinking work the card describes, so **entry roles** will thin out.
I'm well placed: good with tools and good at **explaining numbers**.
do: Build **projects** like a data analysis of local shop prices.
Apply for **placements** in my second year at firms that value tools plus business.
Leave the **call centre** if it shrinks.
feel: A bit **buzzy**: exciting, but I know exciting isn't the same as safe.
S1.quote: A tool is like a calculator. You still have to know when the answer looks wrong.
fieldNote: She treats the change as **a skill problem** she can solve, with some evidence from job boards.
Her main edge is explaining numbers to people.
Will drop the call centre rather than wait for it to shrink.

steps.text: Build a data project on local shop prices for my portfolio
Start a small tutoring website for maths pupils
Apply for second-year placements at firms that use AI tools
Take a statistics module beyond the course minimum

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. That one's called AGI by 2028. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need serious planning right now. Two years isn't enough for governments, so I'd push for a plan to help people with income. I'd say it online and at the student union, because I think people my age need to speak up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the scenario where my degree is at risk. If AI does all thinking work as well as a person but cheaper, why hire an economics graduate? I'd have debt and no obvious job. I'm adaptive, but even I couldn't do much with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move quickly. I'd ask the course office whether I can add a practical module, and I'd start building skills that robots reach later, like care work and project management. I'd keep the tutoring, because pupils still want a human. And I'd talk to Mum's care manager about whether there's a route into healthcare management.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but also focused. I'd have a list, and I'd start on it on day one. I'd probably cry once, and then I'd try to do something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very fast. What would you drop and what would you keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop social things that cost money and spend more time on skills. I'd keep the tutoring and my savings pot, and I'd keep the degree unless it clearly stopped making sense. Quitting too early would also be a risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mum and Grandad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mum and Grandad the truth and that I'm making a plan. Grandad would say I should look for a safe job in the council, and he'd be partly right. Mum would say she'd help, and I'd say no, because she's already working hard.

say: I'd say we need **serious planning** now, with a plan to help people with income.
I'd say it online and at the student union.
think: This is the scenario where my **degree is at risk**: why hire an economics graduate?
Even I couldn't do much with **debt and no job**.
do: Ask the course office about adding a **practical module**.
Build skills robots reach later, like **care work** and project management.
Keep the **tutoring** and the savings pot.
feel: **Scared** but focused: I'd write a list and start on day one.
S2.quote: If AI does all thinking work as well as a person but cheaper, why hire an economics graduate?
fieldNote: She is **adaptive** and starts planning at once, but this is the scenario that hits her field directly.
She uses hands-on and care work as the delayed-robot route, which fits the card.
Protects her mother by refusing help.

steps.text: Ask the course office about adding a practical module
Talk to Mum's care manager about healthcare management routes
Post and speak at the student union for an income plan
Keep the tutoring and the savings pot going

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. That one's called AGI by 2031. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if people act now. I'd back training funds and say universities should add AI skills to every course. I'd tell my friends to practise now, while the pressure is low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's much better. I'd graduate in 2029 and work for two years before AGI. That gives me a bit of money and a job on my CV. I'm still anxious, because the end point is the same, but I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree with a focus on data and strategy, and I'd take a placement year. I'd start a small tutoring business with a few other students and a website. I'd save enough to have six months of cover by graduation, and I'd keep experimenting with every new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Positive but alert. I like having time to try things. I'd probably feel more excited than scared on most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years puts you in work before the AGI date. What does that give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to build and run a small business, because that's a skill that keeps working when jobs change. Also how to check the work of AI, the way an auditor does, since people will still need someone to take responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd teach yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be firefighting. With five I can test, fail a bit and adjust. I'd say that's a better way to learn.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** if people act now, and universities should add AI skills to every course.
I'd tell friends to practise while the pressure is low.
think: I'd graduate in **2029** and work two years before AGI.
The end point is the same, but I can see a **path**.
do: Focus on **data and strategy** and take a placement year.
Start a small **tutoring business** with other students and a website.
Save **six months** of cover by graduation.
feel: **Positive but alert**, more excited than scared on most days.
S3.quote: With two years I'd be firefighting. With five I can test, fail a bit and adjust.
fieldNote: A longer window turns her into **a builder** rather than a firefighter.
Her business idea is a sensible shield against job losses.
Still honest that the end point is the same.

steps.text: Start a student tutoring business with a simple website
Save six months of cover before graduating
Try one new AI tool a month and keep notes
Take a placement year at a data or strategy team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. That one's called AGI by 2036. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is good news if we use it. I'd want a mix of public training, flexible work and basic support for people who lose jobs. I'd be at the table for that, because I'll be one of the people living with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm not too worried. I'd be twenty-eight and ten years into a career. I'd have time to build a business, save and change direction a couple of times. The risk is complacency, so I'd treat each year as a check-in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, work for a few years in a data or strategy role and start a small venture on the side. I'd put money towards a house for Mum and Grandad, or at least a safe place for them. And I'd keep learning every new tool, because that's how I stay useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. I'd be hopeful and busy. A little nervous about the unknown, but in a normal way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. What would you aim for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Basic income that is easy to claim, free training that fits around work and rules so firms can't dump workers without a plan. And I'd want proper care for older people, since that's the area Mum works in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from governments in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A house for Mum and Grandad would be the real win. They've looked after me. If AI makes things cheaper, that should be possible, and I'd aim for it.

say: I'd say ten years is **good news** if we use it, with public training and support for people who lose jobs.
I'd be at the table for that.
think: I'm **not too worried**: by twenty-eight I'd be ten years into a career.
The risk is **complacency**, so I'd treat each year as a check-in.
do: Work in a **data or strategy** role and start a small venture on the side.
Put money towards a safe **home** for Mum and Grandad.
feel: **Pretty good**: hopeful and busy, and a little nervous in a normal way.
S4.quote: A house for Mum and Grandad would be the real win. They've looked after me.
fieldNote: Ten years makes her **calm**, with family security as the goal.
Wants rules about how firms dump workers.
Her mother's care work shapes what she wants from government.

steps.text: Save towards a safe home for Mum and Grandad
Start a small venture alongside a data role
Keep trying every new AI tool at work
Speak up for easy-to-claim income support

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it lands right as I graduate with a loan and no cushion. What would help is quick retraining that pays a living wage, loan payments that pause if there are no jobs, and honest guidance about which skills last.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe only that students like me aren't scared of this. We're just short of money and cushion. If someone gives us a fair chance, we'll adapt.

headlineQuote: We're just short of money and cushion. If someone gives us a fair chance, we'll adapt.
portrait: Olga is an **18-year-old** economics and business student living with her mum and grandad, working a call-centre shift and tutoring.
She uses AI **every day**, treats it like a calculator, and shows classmates how.
She is **uneasy** in most scenarios and alarmed when AGI is two years away, but starts planning at once.
Her goal is a safe home for her **family**, and ten years makes her calm.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario: it lands as she graduates with a loan and no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: Quick **retraining** that pays a living wage, loan pauses if jobs vanish and honest guidance on lasting skills.
